title: Credentials from Password Stores: Keychain
summary: The macOS Keychain Services system stores account names, passwords, private keys, certificates, payment data and secure notes across three collections: the login keychain for the user, the system keychain for items shared by the host, and the local items keychain used for iCloud synchronisation. It is a sub-technique of Credentials from Password Stores because the target is this specific store, and the accessible paths are the database files under the user, system and network library directories, the Keychain Access application and the security command line utility. An unlocked login keychain can be dumped in bulk, and because its protection key derives from the logged-in user's password, an adversary who already holds that password or has persuaded the store to unlock can read the contents. Removal of the store files is itself a signal: a copied login keychain shows up as an unexpected file read or an out-of-place backup copy in a temporary directory.

beginner.definition: Keychain is the password store built into macOS. It remembers website logins, saved Wi-Fi passwords, certificates and private notes for you. This technique is when an attacker takes those items out of Keychain. It is one specific type of the wider password store technique.
beginner.whyItMatters: Keychain holds a wide mix of secrets, not just website logins. One copy can expose email, network and development credentials. Most of it is protected by your Mac login password, so a stolen password is very serious. Attackers also target Keychain early because it unlocks later steps.
howItWorks: macOS keeps its Keychain files in a few library folders on the local disk.
There is a login keychain for you and a system keychain for the whole computer.
The login keychain is normally unlocked using your own Mac login password.
The built-in security command can list and print stored items in bulk.
An unlocked keychain lets an attacker read logins, private keys and certificates.
Attackers often copy the keychain file and work on those copies elsewhere.
beginner.example: Think of a caretaker's key cupboard in a large building. One hook holds the master key to the shared boiler room, others hold spare keys labelled for each office. The cupboard door opens with the caretaker's own code. Anyone who learns that one code holds every labelled key in the building, not just the one they needed.
takeaways: Anyone with your Mac login password can usually open your login keychain.
Alert on the security command reading stored secrets in bulk.
Look for keychain files copied into temporary, upload or backup folders.

objectives: Explain what macOS Keychain stores and where its files live.
Describe the difference between the login, system and local items keychains.
Explain how this sub-technique relates to the parent password store technique.
Identify the commands and file copies that indicate Keychain access.
Recommend monitoring and account hardening that limit Keychain theft.
